newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Bank of Portugal denies it laundered Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Portugal denies it laundered Nazi gold.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal on Monday confirmed a magazine report that it had received gold from Nazi Germany but rejected the implication that it had laundered or hidden stolen assets.

"There is nothing that would implicate the Bank of Portugal in any laundering operation," a central bank spokesman told Reuters when asked to confirm the article in the October 28 edition of Newsweek.

The U.S. magazine said that, while the Swiss may have borne the blame for laundering Nazi gold, other countries were involved in moving and hiding assets stolen mainly from Jews and keeping them from their rightful owners afterwards.
It said Portugal might have been the recipient of the largest amount of stolen gold which had not been accounted for.

The bank spokesman said: "During the Second World War our (gold) reserves did grow but this was because we were selling goods and services, such as (the strategic metal) wolfram which is used in explosives, to Germany. They had no proper currency with which to pay so we took gold."
Asked if the gold might have been stolen from Jews, he said: "How could you tell ? Gold has no race."
He said there were probably a few bars bearing the Nazi swastika in the central bank's vaults but he had never seen them.

Portugal was officially neutral during the war but right-wing dictator Antonio Salazar was thought to sympathise with the Nazis. He provoked international outrage when he ordered flags to be flown at half mast on Adolf Hitler's death.

The Bank of Portugal sold hundreds of tonnes of gold after the country's 1974 revolution, which overthrew the Salazar regime, in order to meet foreign debt payments. But the bank's spokesman said the Nazi gold had probably been sold long before that.
